items.title: The Satavahanas (Andhras) — Deccan's First Great Kingdom
items.body:
## Who Were the Satavahanas?

- The Satavahanas emerged as the **most significant regional power in the Deccan** after the decline of the Mauryan Empire, around the **2nd century BCE**.
- Known as **Andhras in the Puranas**, they built the **first major kingdom in the Deccan**, marking the transition from Mauryan control to regional powers.
- Their realm covered modern **Andhra Pradesh, Maharashtra, Karnataka, Telangana, and Madhya Pradesh** — of direct relevance to Andhra Pradesh's early history.
- **Capital cities: Pratishthana (Paithan)** in Maharashtra and **Amaravati** in Andhra Pradesh (Krishna valley).
- Politically they acted as a **bridge between North and South India**, integrating local Deccan culture with northern traditions.

figure.alt: Map of the Satavahana Empire in the Deccan with Pratishthana and Amaravati marked
figure.caption: The Satavahana Empire spanned the Deccan with centres at Pratishthana (Paithan) and Amaravati, bridging north and south India.

keyPoints: Most significant Deccan power after the Mauryas (c. 2nd century BCE).
Called Andhras in the Puranas; built the first major Deccan kingdom.
Ruled modern AP, Maharashtra, Karnataka, Telangana and MP.
Twin capitals: Pratishthana (Paithan) and Amaravati.
Acted as a political and cultural bridge between North and South India.
items.mnemonic: Andhras of the Deccan — two capitals: 'Paithan in the west, Amaravati in the east'.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Post Mauryan - Satavahanas (Introduction to the Satavahana Dynasty)

items.title: Simuka — Founder of the Dynasty
items.body:
## Simuka (c. 60 BCE – 37 BCE)

- **Simuka founded the Satavahana dynasty**, laying its foundations by defeating local rulers in **Maharashtra and Andhra Pradesh**.
- He built early power through **alliances with the Rathikas and Bhojakas**, local warrior tribes.
- He is **mentioned in the Naneghat inscription** as the first significant ruler of the dynasty.
- His reign marked the **end of Shunga control in the Deccan**.
- Simuka was **succeeded by his brother, Kanha (Krishna)**.
keyPoints: Simuka is the founder of the Satavahana dynasty.
Defeated local rulers in Maharashtra and Andhra Pradesh.
Allied with the Rathikas and Bhojakas.
Mentioned in the Naneghat inscription; ended Shunga control in the Deccan.
Succeeded by his brother Kanha (Krishna).
items.mnemonic: Founder Simuka — 'Started with the Rathikas & Bhojakas, named in Naneghat'.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Post Mauryan - Satavahanas (Simuka – Founder of the Satavahana Dynasty)

items.title: Satakarni I — Lord of Dakshinapatha
items.body:
## Satakarni I

- **Satakarni I expanded the empire** into the **Malwa and Narmada** regions by defeating local rulers.
- Known as the **Lord of Dakshinapatha** (the southern route) — a title recorded in the **Naneghat inscription** written by his wife, **Queen Nayanika (Naganika)**.
- He performed **two Ashvamedha (horse) sacrifices**, symbolising his sovereignty.
- The **Hathigumpha inscription of Kharavela** (of Kalinga) mentions his engagement/conflict with Satakarni I.
keyPoints: Expanded into Malwa and the Narmada valley.
Titled 'Lord of Dakshinapatha' (southern route).
Naneghat inscription written by his queen Nayanika (Naganika).
Performed two Ashvamedha sacrifices to assert sovereignty.
Mentioned in the Hathigumpha inscription of Kharavela of Kalinga.
items.mnemonic: Satakarni I = 'Dakshinapatha lord who ran two Ashvamedhas' — remembered by Queen Nayanika at Naneghat.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Post Mauryan - Satavahanas (Satakarni I – The Lord of Dakshinapatha)

items.title: Hala — Patron of Literature
items.body:
## Hala (c. 20 CE – 24 CE)

- Hala is best known for compiling the **Gatha Saptasati** (Gaha Sattasai) — a **Maharashtri Prakrit anthology of love poems**.
- He **promoted literature and the arts** and is recognised in the **Matsya Purana**.
- His reign was **peaceful**, focused on internal development and literary contribution rather than military conquest.
keyPoints: Compiled the Gatha Saptasati, a Maharashtri Prakrit anthology of love poems.
Remembered as a patron of literature; mentioned in the Matsya Purana.
His reign was peaceful, centred on culture rather than conquest.
items.mnemonic: Hala the poet-king — 'Gatha Saptasati = 700 love verses in Prakrit'.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Post Mauryan - Satavahanas (Hala – Patron of Literature)

items.title: Gautamiputra Satakarni — The Greatest Satavahana
items.body:
## Gautamiputra Satakarni (c. 106 CE – 130 CE)

- Regarded as the **most powerful Satavahana ruler**, he **revived the empire's strength** by defeating the **Shakas, Pahlavas, and Yavanas**.
- His achievements were inscribed in the **Nasik Prashasti** by his mother, **Gautami Balashri**, highlighting his conquests and patronage of Brahmanism.
- He notably **defeated the Shaka king Nahapana** and **restored the pride of Brahmins**; he is called **Ekabrahmana (the unique Brahmin)** in the Nasik Prashasti.
- His empire stretched from **Malwa, Saurashtra, and Konkan to Vidarbha and the Krishna River** in the south.
- Despite his focus on Brahmanism, he **made land grants to Buddhist monks**, promoting religious harmony.

figure.alt: Illustrative banner depicting a Satavahana warrior king with the title Satavahana Dynasty
figure.caption: Gautamiputra Satakarni revived Satavahana power, defeating the Shakas, Pahlavas and Yavanas — celebrated in the Nasik Prashasti of Gautami Balashri.

keyPoints: Greatest/most powerful Satavahana ruler; revived the empire.
Defeated the Shakas, Pahlavas and Yavanas — including the Shaka king Nahapana.
Nasik Prashasti inscribed by his mother Gautami Balashri.
Called Ekabrahmana ('the unique Brahmin'); restored Brahmin pride.
Empire from Malwa/Saurashtra/Konkan to Vidarbha and the Krishna River.
Still made land grants to Buddhist monks — religious harmony.
items.mnemonic: Gautamiputra = 'Greatest' — beat the 3 foreigners (Shakas, Pahlavas, Yavanas); his mother Gautami Balashri wrote the Nasik Prashasti.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Post Mauryan - Satavahanas (Gautamiputra Satakarni – The Reviver of Satavahana Power)

items.title: Vashishtiputra Pulumavi & Yajna Sri Satakarni
items.body:
## Later Great Rulers

### Vashishtiputra Pulumavi (c. 130 CE – 154 CE)
- Extended the empire's **southern borders to the mouth of the Krishna River**.
- Issued **coins bearing ship motifs**, indicating efforts to promote **overseas trade**.
- His **marriage to the daughter of Rudradaman I**, a Shaka king, is mentioned in the **Junagadh inscription** — an example of marital diplomacy.

### Yajna Sri Satakarni (c. 165 CE – 194 CE)
- The **last great ruler**, he **recovered Malwa and Konkan from the Shakas**.
- His **coins with ship images** reflect the importance of **maritime trade**.
- After his reign the empire declined and fragmented into smaller kingdoms.
keyPoints: Pulumavi pushed the southern frontier to the mouth of the Krishna River.
Pulumavi's ship-motif coins point to overseas trade.
Pulumavi married Rudradaman I's daughter (Junagadh inscription) — marital diplomacy.
Yajna Sri Satakarni was the last great ruler; recovered Malwa and Konkan.
Yajna Sri's ship coins underline the era's maritime trade.
items.mnemonic: Pulumavi = 'ship coins + Rudradaman's daughter (Junagadh)'; Yajna Sri = 'last great, ships again'.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Post Mauryan - Satavahanas (Vashisthiputra Pulumavi; Yajna Sri Satakarni)

items.title: Matronymic Names & the Position of Women
items.body:
## Naming After Mothers

- The Satavahanas followed a **matronymic tradition**: kings were often **named after their mothers**, indicating the **importance of women** in Satavahana society.
- The names literally reflect this — **Gautami-putra** ('son of Gautami') and **Vashishti-putra** ('son of Vashishti').
- **Women held influential roles**: **Nayanika (Naganika)** served as **regent** for her minor son, and **Gautami Balashri** authored the **Nasik Prashasti** glorifying Gautamiputra Satakarni.
keyPoints: Matronymic tradition: kings named after their mothers (e.g. Gautami-putra, Vashishti-putra).
Reflects the high status of women in Satavahana society.
Nayanika (Naganika) acted as regent for her minor son.
Gautami Balashri authored the Nasik Prashasti.
items.mnemonic: 'Putra of the mother' — Gautami-putra, Vashishti-putra: matronymic names.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Post Mauryan - Satavahanas (Social Structure – Matronymic Tradition; Position of Women)

items.title: Administration — Divisions, Feudatories & Officers
items.body:
## Decentralised Governance

- The Satavahanas **retained several Mauryan administrative features** but tailored them to local needs, with **regional control, military governance, and feudal elements**.

### Administrative divisions (largest → smallest)
- **Janapada** (province) → **Rashtra** (sub-province, under a *Rashtrika/Maharathi*) → **Ahara** (district, under *Amatyas/Mahamatras*) → **Vishaya** (sub-division) → **Grama** (village, under a *Gramani* or *Gaulmika*).

### Feudatory grades
- **Rajas** (highest; minted coins in their own names), **Mahabhojas** (Thane–Kolaba, western Deccan), and **Maharathis** (Poona district).

### Key officers
- **Senapati** (commander & provincial governor), **Rajjuka** (revenue), **Bhandagarika** (treasurer), **Paniyagharika** (waterworks), **Karmantika** (public works), and **Avesanika** (foreman of artisans).
keyPoints: Divisions: Janapada > Rashtra > Ahara > Vishaya > Grama.
Three feudatory grades: Rajas (minted coins), Mahabhojas, Maharathis.
Gaulmika/Gramani headed villages; Katakas & Skandhavaras were military camps/cantonments.
Senapati served as both army commander and provincial governor.
Specialist officers: Rajjuka (revenue), Bhandagarika (treasury), Paniyagharika (water), Karmantika (works).
items.mnemonic: Divisions big→small: 'Ja-Ra-A-Vi-Gra' (Janapada, Rashtra, Ahara, Vishaya, Grama).
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Post Mauryan - Satavahanas (Administration – Divisions, Feudatory System, Key Officers)

items.title: Economy, Trade & Coinage
items.body:
## A Trading Powerhouse

- **Agriculture:** the **Krishna–Godavari delta** was a major **rice-producing** region; **paddy transplantation** boosted productivity.
- **Trade routes:** the **Uttarapatha** (northern) and **Dakshinapatha** (southern) routes; key **ports** were **Kalyani, Sopara, Bharuch (Barygaza), and Ganjam**.
- **Coinage:** coins were issued in **lead, copper, and bronze** (potin was also used), carrying **animal motifs and Prakrit inscriptions** in the **Brahmi script**.
- Coins depicting **ships and Chaityas** underline the importance of **maritime trade** — flourishing sea commerce (including with the Roman world, attested by ports like Barygaza) enriched the state.
keyPoints: Krishna–Godavari delta was a major rice bowl; paddy transplantation raised yields.
Trade along Uttarapatha and Dakshinapatha; ports: Kalyani, Sopara, Bharuch, Ganjam.
Coins in lead, copper and bronze with animal motifs and Prakrit (Brahmi) legends.
Ship-and-Chaitya coins reflect thriving maritime trade (incl. Roman contact via Barygaza).
items.mnemonic: Satavahana money = 'Lead & copper coins with ships' — the sea-trade dynasty.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Post Mauryan - Satavahanas (Economy – Agriculture, Trade and Commerce, Coinage)

items.title: Art & Architecture — The Amaravati School
items.body:
## Deccan Buddhist Art (AP relevance)

- The **Amaravati Stupa** in **Andhra Pradesh** — begun in the **3rd century BCE** — depicts **Jataka tales and events from the life of the Buddha**, and was **discovered by Colin Mackenzie**. It gives its name to the celebrated **Amaravati School of Art**.
- **Nagarjunakonda Stupa** (Andhra Pradesh), later patronised by the **Ikshvaku rulers**, is known for its **Buddhist carvings**.
- In Maharashtra, the **Karle Chaitya** is the **largest rock-cut Chaitya hall**, and **Ajanta Caves 9 and 10** were developed under **Satavahana patronage**.

figure.alt: Map of the Satavahana Empire showing Amaravati in the Krishna valley of Andhra Pradesh
figure.caption: Amaravati (Krishna valley, Andhra Pradesh) gave its name to the Amaravati School of Art — a hallmark of Satavahana-era Buddhist sculpture.

keyPoints: Amaravati Stupa (AP): Jataka tales & Buddha's life; discovered by Colin Mackenzie — namesake of the Amaravati School of Art.
Nagarjunakonda (AP): Buddhist carvings, later patronised by the Ikshvakus.
Karle Chaitya (Maharashtra): largest rock-cut Chaitya hall.
Ajanta Caves 9 and 10 developed under Satavahana patronage.
items.mnemonic: AP's Buddhist gems — 'Amaravati + Nagarjunakonda'; Maharashtra's rock-cut — 'Karle + Ajanta 9-10'.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Post Mauryan - Satavahanas (Art and Architecture During the Satavahana Period)

items.title: Religion, Society & Land Grants to Brahmins
items.body:
## Brahmanism with Buddhist Patronage

- The Satavahanas were **Brahmins** who performed **Vedic sacrifices** such as the **Ashvamedha and Rajasuya**, yet they also **promoted Buddhism by making land grants to Buddhist monks**.
- They pioneered the practice of **granting land (including to Brahmins and monasteries)** with fiscal and administrative privileges — an important precedent in Indian history.
- **Society followed the Varna system**, but **merchants and artisans gained importance** because of thriving trade.
- Women were influential (matronymic names; regents like Nayanika), reflecting a relatively high social status.
keyPoints: Rulers were Brahmins performing Vedic sacrifices (Ashvamedha, Rajasuya).
Simultaneously patronised Buddhism through land grants to monks.
Early practice of land grants (to Brahmins/monasteries) with privileges.
Varna society, but traders and artisans rose in importance due to trade.
items.mnemonic: Satavahana faith balance — 'Brahmin kings, Buddhist land grants'.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Ancient History: Post Mauryan - Satavahanas (Religion and Society During the Satavahana Period)

items.title: Decline & Successor Kingdoms
items.body:
## The End of Satavahana Rule

- **Internal weaknesses:** the dynasty declined under **ineffective rulers after Yajna Sri Satakarni**.
- **Feudal fragmentation:** the rise of **feudatories** and the loss of central authority further divided the empire.
- **Successor kingdoms:**
  - **Ikshvakus** in **Andhra Pradesh** (Krishna–Guntur region).
  - **Abhiras and Chutus** in **Maharashtra/western Deccan**.
  - **Pallavas** in **Tamil Nadu**.
keyPoints: Decline set in with weak rulers after Yajna Sri Satakarni.
Rising feudatories and lost central authority fragmented the empire.
Ikshvakus succeeded in Andhra Pradesh.
Abhiras and Chutus rose in Maharashtra; Pallavas in Tamil Nadu.
